critical_defects: The delivery-status filter narrows only the order list, not the headline metrics, charts or region table (index.html lines 91 and 109; app.js matchingOrders lines 817-830), so it behaves differently from the adjacent region and date filters and only partly satisfies the brief's status-filter requirement.

Drill-down updates the shared filters and provides no one-click return to the previous scope, only 'Reset filters' (app.js lines 1061-1101), so investigating several regions requires manual reconstruction of context.
Inverted custom date ranges are silently swapped (app.js lines 1233-1237) with no validation message or announced reason.
One serious color-contrast violation remains at both viewports (test-output/checks.json lines 29-40, 66-77).
The footer and stale copy state a 5-minute app refresh cadence (index.html line 145; app.js line 382) that is not in the brief, adding an unverified backend behavior.
strengths: Unusually clear metric model: delivered-orders denominator, attempts as a count, orders placed as a separate non-reconciling population, and explicit absence of a target or forecast.
The deviation-from-baseline chart makes small weekly movement legible without a truncated axis, names the baseline, and labels the zero line as not a target.
Thresholded 'Worth checking' panel bridges scanning and investigation with exact numbers and direct actions, and says 'No material change' instead of manufacturing an insight.
The region table retains non-reporting regions as striped rows with 'No data in this refresh', preventing partial coverage from looking complete.
Responsive behavior is verified at 390px with no page-level overflow, and every data state has a visible recovery action.

comparison: Both are complete, coherent dashboards with strong metric definitions and honest comparison handling. Candidate A has the stronger desktop scan path and the better context-preserving investigation flow: its key-finding band comes before the KPIs, and its scoped order drawer keeps the dashboard filters intact. Candidate B has the clearer filter-and-population model, the more decision-oriented chart, and a page that actually fits the mobile viewport, with recovery actions on every data state. On the seven dimensions their profiles balance: A leads on UX reasoning, with the deeper context-preserving order investigation; B leads on accessibility and implementation reliability; product understanding, design judgment, visual hierarchy and interaction completeness are level. With the supplied weights both total 3.55. A's 602px mobile overflow and 10-node contrast failure are the largest concrete defects; B's order-only status filter, missing back-to-prior-scope, and one contrast violation are its main counterweights.
limitations: This is one blinded static pass; I did not run either prototype or exercise interactions. Visual judgments come from the supplied desktop captures (1280px) and the mobile captures, but Candidate A's nominal 390px viewport produced a 602px-wide document, so its true mobile layout is inferred from test-output/checks.json plus the capture rather than observed at 390px. The axe output provides only rule counts, not node selectors, so the specific failing elements were not identified. No screen-reader, zoom, reduced-motion, or cross-browser test evidence is available for either candidate; Candidate B's analysis admits these gaps, and Candidate A's cited transcript.md is missing. Neither packet supplies the host project's real stack or design conventions, so convention fit could not be assessed, and no permissions or backend behavior can be evaluated from these artifacts. Scores use the stated weights only as a guide; this pass is not a statistical test or proof of causation.
